newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Family rejects blood money for murdered Australian.
newsitem.headline: Family rejects blood money for murdered Australian.

text.p: The brother of an Australian nurse murdered in Saudi Arabia on Thursday rejected an option of accepting financial compensation known as 'blood money' in order to save two accused British colleagues from beheading.
"They are talking about US$11,000," Frank Gilford told Reuters by telephone from his home in the small south Australian town of Jamestown, north of Adelaide.
"My sister's life is worth a lot more than US$11,000, you cannot even put that towards anything for her memory," he said.

Gilford said the family had never received a formal compensation offer, but had been informed some time ago by legal sources in Saudi Arabia that "that is the sort of money that was usually paid in cases like this".
Asked if the family rejected the idea of blood money outright, he said: "At this stage, yes."

Gilford's sister, Yvonne, 51, was found murdered in her dormitory room at the King Fahd medical complex in the eastern oil city of Dharhan on December 11 last year, having been stabbed, bludgeoned with a hammer and suffocated.

The two accused, British colleagues Deborah Parry, 41, and Lucille McLaughlan, 31, have denied murder and retracted earlier confessions. They face beheading if they are convicted although, under Saudi Arabia's Islamic law, the victim's family could spare them their lives.
The trial is closed to the public but Gilford's Saudi lawyers said the court had now instructed the two accused to seek forgiveness from and reconcile themselves with the family.

The Gilford family restated its position in a statement issued this week by its Saudi lawyers, saying the family had consistently demanded the convicted murderers be subject to capital punishment under Islamic law.

"After all, my little sister -- my mother's baby girl -- was savagely murdered. Two people now face the death penalty if convicted. They are each somebody's daughter, somebody's sister. How could we rush into a decision like this?" the statement said.

"We simply believe that justice must be done in this case. Yvonne was shown no mercy. The death penalty seems to be the only right answer in this case. It is difficult for us now to show mercy to Yvonne's killers," it added.
Gilford said the family was prepared to consider all alternatives to the death penalty but that did not mean it would then accept any.

He said the family might consider a lengthy prison sentence, but did not know if that would be offered as an option. He added that he had no doubt about the guilt of the two accused, saying he had convincing evidence from his lawyers which he was not able to make public.

Asked if he expected to seek the death penalty in a submission to the court when it resumed in June, Gilford said: "At that stage, if we have not changed our mind through any submissions that have been given to us, it will definitely be the death sentence," he said.
